Hockey Art Ladder

One 3 vs 3 ice hockey arena, 60 by 30 m, lit three ways. Nine reference stills: three tiers tied to the game's difficulty tiers, three environment variants in each. Pick one variant per tier below.

Reference studies only. Under contest rule 7(h) these images are never imported into any Unreal project, never used as textures, backdrops or tracing sources, and never shipped. The chosen look is rebuilt from scratch in the engine during the jam. Generated 2026-11-11 with Codex image generation, one image per run, no reference images attached. Feasibility notes assume Unreal Engine 5.9 on one RTX 4090 and come from general UE 5.x knowledge; hours and frame times are estimates, not measurements. A generated still shows a finished look and hides the cost of dressing such as stands, windows and skylines.

L1 Daylight toy rink

M1 regular hockey

Warm sun and sky light, bloom about 0.2, clean pale ice. Cost class: cheap.

Costlow

Sun plus sky light, Lumen or baked bounce, one post volume. Soft shadows over six figures and white boards cost the most; variant b adds rect lights, variant c a stable depth-of-field tilt.

Frame-rate risklow

Medium Lumen with a fixed light count should hold 60 fps on a GTX 1660 or RTX 3060 at 1080p; baked lighting plus one cascaded shadow map is the fallback.

Readabilitylow

Best of the three. Near-black puck on pale ice and deep blue against warm orange. Give the puck a slightly oversized radius and a soft contact shadow.

L2 Night arena

M2 raw play, tackles

Dim cool sky, three to five spots, emissive trim in team colours, bloom 0.8 to 1.0. Cost class: cheap to medium.

Costmed

Same rig as L1 with the sun swapped for spots and the trim emissive raised. Each shadow-casting spot costs virtual shadow map time, so keep to four and fake the rest with additive cones.

Frame-rate riskmed

Low to medium. Four shadowed spots plus mild bloom is close to L1; volumetric fog is the real risk, so make it optional or low resolution.

Readabilitymed

The puck is the weak point on mid-dark ice. Add a thin emissive ring or light-grey edge band that is already on in L1, so nothing is rebuilt.

L3 Full neon

M3 boost packages

Cyan and magenta emissive strips, ground fog, bloom 1.5 or more, wet low-roughness ice, glowing pickups. Cost class: expensive.

Costhigh

Ray-traced reflections on a full-screen glossy ice plane are nearly every pixel, then bloom and fog together. The path tracer is for stills, not play.

Frame-rate riskhigh

High with hardware RT. A GTX 1660 has no RT hardware and an RTX 3060 likely falls well below 60 fps at 1080p. Ship the reflection method as a quality switch defaulted by detected hardware.

Reflection fallbackmed

Order: hardware RT, then screen-space or Lumen software reflections, then a fake mirror (strips and goal frames duplicated under the ice with a fresnel fade), last a fixed capture plus gloss map. Bloom and emissive strips carry most of the look in every step.

Readabilityhigh

Neon, reflections and bloom compete with the puck. Give the puck an emissive core, thin halo or short trail, dim the painted ice lines, and keep the trim palette distinct from the jersey palette.

What stays constant, what changes

  • Geometry: rink with rounded corners, boards and glass or fence panels, two 4 m goals, face-off lines and circles as decals, the figures, the puck, the pickup meshes (present from the start, hidden until L3), and the dressing of the chosen variant.
  • Materials: one ice master, one plastic and boards master, one emissive trim. Emissive and roughness parameters exist from L1 and are driven per tier through a material parameter collection. Jersey colours (deep blue, warm orange) never change.
  • Camera: one high three-quarter camera keeping both goals in frame, same field of view, framing and height in all three tiers.
  • Gameplay-facing values: collision, physics, ice friction, the puck rim and the size of everything.

Reading across: L1 to L2 is mostly a lighting swap plus post once the master materials exist. L2 to L3 is the emissive and reflection step and carries nearly all of the risk. Build L1 and L2 first and treat L3 as an add-on with its own fallback switch. Across variants the camera is similar but not identical (c is closer, a shows more surroundings), and the generator invented different net details between images, which a real build would not do.
